l: Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 27
s: Ezekiel, addressed as 'son of man,' is commanded by the LORD to take up a lamentation over Tyre and to deliver the Lord GOD's message to the city.

l: lamentation over Tyre, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 27
s: The lamentation is commissioned by the LORD in verse 2 and takes the form of a long description of Tyre as a splendid ship and trading power. It also anticipates the mourners' own lament: 'Who is there like Tyre, like her who is brought to silence in the middle of the sea?'

l: ship of Tyre, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 27
s: Tyre is depicted as a ship whose planks are cypress from Senir, mast is Lebanon cedar, oars are Bashan oak, benches are ivory inlaid in cypress, and sail is embroidered Egyptian linen with blue and purple awning from Elishah. Its rowers bring it into great waters, where the east wind breaks it in the heart of the seas.

l: Tyre's trade and merchandise, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 27
s: Many nations traded with Tyre, including Tarshish with silver, iron, tin, and lead; Javan, Tubal, and Meshech with persons and bronze vessels; Togarmah with horses and mules; Judah and Israel with wheat, honey, oil, and balm; and Sheba and Raamah with spices, stones, and gold. This trade filled many peoples and enriched kings, but the merchandise falls into the seas in the day of Tyre's ruin.

l: Tyre's mariners and crew (Tyre), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 27
s: Tyre's rowers came from Sidon and Arvad, its pilots were its own wise men, and the old men of Gebal repaired seams. Its army included men of Persia, Lud, Put, and Arvad. When the ship falls, the mariners and pilots come ashore, cry bitterly, cast dust on their heads, wear sackcloth, and mourn for Tyre.

l: Tyre's downfall, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 27
s: The east wind breaks Tyre in the heart of the seas, and its riches, wares, crew, and company fall into the sea in the day of its ruin. The pasture lands shake at the pilots' cry, island inhabitants are astonished, kings are horribly afraid, and merchants hiss at Tyre, which has come to a terrible end and will be no more.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 28
s: The LORD instructs the prophet to speak against the prince of Tyre, who claims to be a god and is proud of the wisdom and riches he has gained through trading; the LORD declares that foreign strangers will bring him down to a violent death. A lamentation is then taken up over the king of Tyre, who was once perfect, wise, and beautiful in Eden, the garden of God, and an anointed covering cherub on God's holy mountain. Unrighteousness and violence from his commerce led to his being cast out, laid before kings, and burned to ashes by a fire from within him. The LORD then sets his face against Sidon, promising pestilence, bloodshed, and the sword so that they will know he is the LORD. The chapter closes with a promise that Israel will be gathered, freed from scornful neighbors, and will dwell securely in the land given to Jacob.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 28
s: The LORD speaks to the prophet, condemning the prince and king of Tyre and declaring he is against Sidon. He says he will be glorified and sanctified through his judgments, and promises to gather Israel and give them security in their land so that all will know he is the LORD.

l: prince of Tyre, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 28
s: The prince of Tyre is accused of lifting up his heart, claiming 'I am a god' and sitting in God's seat, though he is only a man. Because of his wisdom and riches from trading, he is told that strangers will bring him to the pit and he will die the death of the uncircumcised.

l: Tyre, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 28
s: Tyre is the city whose prince and king are addressed, set in the middle of the seas. Its rulers' wealth was gained through wisdom and commerce, and the judgment spoken against them is that they will be brought down and destroyed.

l: king of Tyre, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 28
s: A lamentation is raised over the king of Tyre, who is described as the seal of full measure, full of wisdom, perfect in beauty, in Eden adorned with precious stones, and an anointed covering cherub on God's holy mountain. Unrighteousness, violence from his commerce, and a heart lifted up because of his beauty led to his being cast out, laid before kings, and turned to ashes by a fire from within him, so that he becomes a terror and exists no more.

l: strangers and wicked nations, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 28
s: The LORD says he will bring strangers, 'the terrible of the nations,' against the prince of Tyre. They will draw swords against the beauty of his wisdom, defile his brightness, and bring him down to a violent death.

l: Sidon, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 28
s: The prophet is told to set his face toward Sidon and prophesy against it. The LORD declares he is against Sidon and will send pestilence, blood in its streets, and the sword on every side, so that they will know he is the LORD.

l: Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 28
s: The house of Israel will no longer suffer a pricking brier or hurting thorn from scornful neighbors. The LORD will gather them from the peoples among whom they are scattered and show himself holy among them, and they will dwell securely in their own land given to Jacob, building houses and planting vineyards.

l: judgment on Tyre and Sidon, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 28
s: The LORD pronounces judgment on Tyre's prince and king through foreign swords, death, a devouring fire, and ashes, and on Sidon through pestilence, bloodshed, and the sword. The purpose stated is that they will know he is the LORD and that he is sanctified, and the judgments also end the scorn Israel suffered from those around them.

l: pride and wealth from commerce, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 28
s: The prince of Tyre's heart is lifted up because of riches gained by wisdom and trading, leading him to claim divinity. The king's abundant commerce filled him with violence and unrighteousness, profaned his sanctuaries, and led to his downfall.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 29
s: In Chapter 29 the LORD tells Ezekiel to prophesy against Pharaoh king of Egypt, who is called a great monster in his rivers for claiming the river as his own. The LORD says he will hook Pharaoh and cast him into the wilderness as food for animals and birds, and will bring a sword on Egypt and make it a desolation from the tower of Seveneh to the border of Ethiopia for forty years. The Egyptians will be scattered, then gathered back to Pathros as a lowly kingdom that will never again rule the nations or be Israel's confidence. A later word, dated the twenty-seventh year, says Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon received no wages from his hard service against Tyre, so the LORD gives him Egypt as payment. The chapter ends with the LORD promising to make a horn sprout for the house of Israel and to open Ezekiel's mouth among them.

l: Pharaoh king of Egypt, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 29
s: Pharaoh is addressed as the great monster lying in his rivers, who claimed the river as his own and made it for himself. The LORD declares he is against him, will put hooks in his jaws, pull him out with the fish sticking to his scales, and cast him into the open wilderness as food for animals and birds.

l: Egypt, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 29
s: Egypt is to suffer a sword that cuts off man and animal, becoming a desolation and waste from the tower of Seveneh to the border of Ethiopia, with no one passing through. It is later restored in Pathros as the lowest of the kingdoms, and is given to Nebuchadnezzar as wages for his army.

l: Egyptians, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 29
s: The Egyptians are to be scattered among the nations for forty years and then gathered from the peoples where they were scattered. They will return to Pathros, the land of their birth, as a lowly kingdom, and will know that the LORD is the LORD because they were a staff of reed to Israel.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 29
s: The LORD speaks to Ezekiel on two dates and declares he is against Pharaoh and Egypt, promising judgment so that all will know he is the LORD. He also reverses Egypt's captivity after forty years, gives Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar as payment for work done for him, and promises to make a horn sprout for Israel.

l: Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 29
s: Ezekiel, addressed as son of man, is told to set his face against Pharaoh and prophesy against him and all Egypt. He receives two words from the LORD, and is promised that his mouth will be opened among the house of Israel.

l: house of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 29
s: Israel is said to have been leaned on Egypt, which proved a staff of reed that broke and tore their shoulders and paralyzed their thighs. After Egypt's judgment it will no longer be Israel's confidence or bring iniquity to memory, and the LORD will cause a horn to sprout for Israel.

l: king of Babylon, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 29
s: Nebuchadnezzar made his army serve a great service against Tyre, leaving every head bald and every shoulder worn, yet received no wages from it. The LORD therefore gives him the land of Egypt to carry off its multitude, plunder and prey as wages for his army.

l: forty years of desolation, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 29
s: Egypt's land and cities are to be a desolation for forty years, uninhabited and unpassed by man or animal, while the Egyptians are scattered among the nations. At the end of the forty years the LORD will gather them and return them to Pathros.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 30
s: In Ezekiel 30 the LORD commands the prophet to wail over the coming day of the LORD, a day of clouds and a time of the nations, when a sword will fall on Egypt and its allies Ethiopia, Put, Lud, Cub and others. The LORD names Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon as the agent who will destroy Egypt's multitude, dry up its rivers, and fill the land with the slain. Egyptian idols, cities including Memphis, Pathros, Zoan, No, Sin, Aven, Pibeseth and Tehaphnehes, and its princes are to be destroyed or taken into captivity. In a second oracle dated the seventh day of the first month of the eleventh year, the LORD says he has broken Pharaoh's arm and will break both arms, making the sword fall from his hand. He will strengthen the king of Babylon with his sword and scatter the Egyptians among the nations, so that they will know that he is the LORD.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 30
s: The LORD commands the prophet to wail over the coming day and declares he will bring a sword on Egypt, set fire to it, destroy its idols, and pour out his wrath. He says he has broken Pharaoh's arm, will strengthen the king of Babylon and put his own sword in his hand, and will scatter the Egyptians so that they know he is the LORD.

l: Egypt, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 30
s: Egypt is to suffer a sword, anguish, fire and desolation, with its multitude cut off, its rivers dried, and its land sold into the hand of evil men. Its allies Ethiopia, Put, Lud, Cub and others fall with it, and its cities from Memphis to Tehaphnehes are struck. Its people will be scattered among the nations and dispersed through the countries.

l: king of Babylon, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 30
s: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon is named as the one by whose hand the LORD will make Egypt's multitude cease. He and his people, called the terrible of the nations, will draw their swords against Egypt and fill the land with the slain. The LORD will strengthen his arms and put the LORD's sword in his hand.

l: multitude of Pharaoh, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 30
s: Pharaoh king of Egypt has had his arm broken by the LORD, and it has not been bound up to become strong enough to hold a sword. The LORD says he is against Pharaoh and will break both his arms, so that the sword falls from his hand and he groans like a mortally wounded man before the king of Babylon.

l: day of the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 30
s: The day of the LORD is described as near, a day of clouds and a time of the nations, to be mourned with the cry 'Alas for the day!' It brings the sword on Egypt, anguish in Ethiopia, and the fall of Egypt's allies.

l: judgment on Egypt, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 30
s: The LORD says he will execute judgments on Egypt through fire, sword and the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, ending its idols, its prince, and its multitude, and striking cities such as Memphis, Zoan, No and Sin. The purpose repeated is that they will know that he is the LORD. A second oracle adds the breaking of Pharaoh's arms and the scattering of the Egyptians among the nations.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 31
s: In the eleventh year, on the first day of the third month, the LORD tells the prophet to address Pharaoh king of Egypt and his multitude, asking whom he resembles in greatness. The LORD answers with an image of the Assyrian as a great cedar in Lebanon, nourished by many waters, sheltering birds, animals and nations, and envied by all the trees of Eden in the garden of God. Because its heart was lifted up in its height, the LORD delivers it to the mighty one of the nations, and foreigners cut it down so that its branches fall across the mountains and valleys and its shadow is abandoned. Its descent to Sheol causes mourning, makes the nations shake, and comforts the trees of Eden in the lower parts of the earth, where its allies also go down to those slain by the sword. The passage ends by telling Pharaoh that he will likewise be brought down among the uncircumcised slain by the sword, declaring that the tree is Pharaoh and all his multitude.

l: Pharaoh king of Egypt, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 31
s: Pharaoh king of Egypt is addressed by the LORD through the prophet and asked whom he is like in his greatness. He is compared to the proud Assyrian cedar, and is told he will be brought down with the trees of Eden to the lower parts of the earth. He will lie among the uncircumcised and those slain by the sword.

l: multitude of Pharaoh, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 31
s: The multitude of Pharaoh is addressed together with Pharaoh and is included in the comparison to the Assyrian cedar. The closing line identifies the tree as Pharaoh and all his multitude, so they share his coming fall to the lower parts of the earth.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 31
s: The LORD speaks to the prophet, commands him to address Pharaoh, and describes how he made the Assyrian beautiful with many branches. Because of its pride, he delivers it into the hand of the mighty one of the nations and drives it out for its wickedness. He causes mourning at its descent to Sheol, makes the nations shake at its fall, and declares that Pharaoh and his multitude will suffer the same end.

l: Assyrian, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 31
s: The Assyrian is described as a cedar in Lebanon of high stature, beautiful and nourished by many waters, under whose shadow great nations lived. Its heart was lifted up in its height, so the LORD delivered it to the mighty one of the nations. It was cut down by foreigners and sent down to Sheol with the slain, including those who had been its arm.

l: cedar in Lebanon (the Assyrian), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 31
s: The cedar is a tree of great height with a top among the thick boughs, fed by deep waters and rivers, and home to birds and animals. It surpassed the cedars, cypresses and pines of the garden of God, and the trees of Eden envied it. It is cut down, its branches scatter across mountains, valleys and watercourses, and birds and animals dwell on its ruin as a warning to other trees not to exalt themselves.

l: Eden, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 31
s: The garden of God is the place whose cedars could not hide the Assyrian cedar and whose cypress and pine trees were not like its branches. No tree there matched its beauty. The trees of Eden in the garden envied it, and later they are brought down to the lower parts of the earth and comforted there.

l: Sheol, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 31
s: Sheol is where the LORD casts the Assyrian down, with those who descend into the pit. Its descent there causes mourning, with the deep covered and the rivers restrained. Those who were the Assyrian's arm also go down to Sheol, to those slain by the sword.

l: fall of the Assyrian, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 31
s: The fall of the Assyrian happens because of its pride and wickedness, when the LORD delivers it to the mighty one of the nations and foreigners cut it off. Its branches fall across the land and the peoples leave its shadow. The fall causes mourning, makes the nations shake, and serves as a warning to the other trees not to exalt themselves, a fate Pharaoh is told he will share.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 32
s: In Ezekiel 32, the LORD commands Ezekiel to take up a lamentation over Pharaoh king of Egypt, who is likened to a young lion of the nations and a monster in the seas. The LORD says he will catch Pharaoh in his net, leave him on the open field for birds and animals, darken the heavens, and bring the sword of the king of Babylon against Egypt, using the ruthless of the nations to destroy its multitude. In a second word, given on the fifteenth day of the same month, Ezekiel is told to wail for Egypt's multitude and cast them down to the pit among the uncircumcised slain by the sword. The chapter lists nations already in Sheol: Asshur, Elam, Meshech, Tubal, Edom, the princes of the north, and the Sidonians, all of whom caused terror in the land of the living and now lie slain. Pharaoh will see them and be comforted, but he and all his multitude will be laid among the uncircumcised slain by the sword.

l: Pharaoh king of Egypt, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 32
s: Pharaoh is the subject of the lamentation, likened to a young lion of the nations yet a monster in the seas who troubled the waters. The LORD says he will net him, cast him on the open field, and lay him among the uncircumcised slain by the sword. Pharaoh will see the other fallen nations and be comforted over his multitude, because the LORD has put his terror in the land of the living.

l: Egypt, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 32
s: Egypt is to be made desolate and waste, with its multitude, pride, and animals destroyed by the sword of the king of Babylon and the mighty ruthless of the nations. Its waters will later run clear like oil, and its multitude is to be cast down to the lower parts of the earth with those who go down into the pit. Through this, they will know that the LORD is the LORD.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 32
s: The LORD gives Ezekiel two words, in the twelfth year on the first and fifteenth days of the month, commanding a lamentation and a wailing over Egypt. He declares he will spread his net over Pharaoh, darken the sky, brandish his sword before many peoples, and bring the destruction of Egypt so that they will know he is the LORD. He has put Pharaoh's terror in the land of the living.

l: king of Babylon, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 32
s: The LORD declares that the sword of the king of Babylon will come on Egypt. It is the instrument by which Egypt's multitude will fall, together with the swords of the mighty, the ruthless of the nations.

l: Asshur, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 32
s: Asshur is in the pit with all her company, her graves set in its uttermost parts and around her. All of them are slain, fallen by the sword, having caused terror in the land of the living.

l: Elam, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 32
s: Elam lies in the lower parts of the earth with all her multitude around her grave, all uncircumcised and slain by the sword. They caused terror in the land of the living and now bear their shame with those who go down to the pit.

l: Meshech, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 32
s: Meshech is in Sheol with all their multitude, their graves around them, all uncircumcised and slain by the sword for having caused terror in the land of the living. They do not lie with the fallen mighty who went down with their weapons of war. Their iniquities are on their bones.

l: Tubal, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 32
s: Tubal is named together with Meshech and their multitude, whose graves are around them, all uncircumcised and slain by the sword. They caused terror in the land of the living and do not lie with the mighty fallen with their weapons.

l: Edom, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 32
s: Edom is there with her kings and all her princes, who in their might are laid with those slain by the sword. They lie with the uncircumcised and with those who go down to the pit.

l: princes of the north, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 32
s: All the princes of the north have gone down with the slain. They are put to shame for the terror they caused by their might, lying uncircumcised with those slain by the sword and bearing their shame with those in the pit.

l: Sidonians, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 32
s: All the Sidonians are named with the princes of the north as having gone down with the slain. They are put to shame in the terror they caused by their might and lie uncircumcised among those slain by the sword.

l: Sheol, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 32
s: Sheol is the place of the dead, called the pit and the lower parts of the earth, where the fallen nations lie uncircumcised, slain by the sword. The strong among the mighty speak out of its middle, and Egypt's multitude is to be cast down into it.

l: lamentation over Pharaoh, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 32
s: The LORD commands Ezekiel to take up this lamentation over Pharaoh king of Egypt, comparing him to a young lion who is really a monster in the seas. The LORD says the daughters of the nations will lament with it over Egypt and all her multitude.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 33
s: The LORD tells Ezekiel (the 'son of man') that he is a watchman for the house of Israel, using a parable of a watchman who either blows the trumpet at the approach of the sword or fails to, so that responsibility for blood falls on the hearer or on the watchman. The LORD declares he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked but wants them to turn and live, and he explains that neither past righteousness nor past wickedness settles a person's fate, since each is judged by his own ways, against the people's charge that his way is not fair. A fugitive from Jerusalem arrives in the twelfth year of the captivity announcing the city's defeat, and Ezekiel's mouth, opened the evening before, is no longer mute. The LORD then rebukes those in the waste places of the land of Israel who claim inheritance because they are many, citing their blood-eating, idolatry, bloodshed and adultery, and promises desolation by sword, beasts and pestilence. The people enjoy Ezekiel like a lovely song but do not act on his words, until events show that a prophet has been among them.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 33
s: The LORD appoints Ezekiel as watchman and declares he has no pleasure in the death of the wicked but wants them to turn and live. He says he will judge each person by his ways and answers the charge of unfairness by turning it back on the people. He promises to make the land desolate so that they will know he is the LORD, and his hand had opened Ezekiel's mouth before the fugitive arrived.

l: Ezekiel (son of man), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 33
s: Ezekiel is set as a watchman for the house of Israel, commanded to speak the LORD's warnings or else bear responsibility for the blood of the wicked. After the escaped fugitive brings news of Jerusalem's defeat, his mouth is opened and he is no longer mute. The people flock to hear him as to a pleasant song but do not obey, and when the prophecy comes to pass they will know a prophet has been among them.

l: house of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 33
s: The house of Israel laments that their transgressions and sins are on them and asks how they can live. The LORD urges them to turn from their evil ways, asks why they will die, and tells them he will judge each according to his ways. They accuse the LORD's way of being unfair, though it is their own way that is not fair.

l: watchman (parable watchman), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 33
s: In the parable, the people of a land set a man as watchman who, on seeing the sword come, should blow the trumpet. If he warns and people ignore it, their blood is on their own heads; if he fails to warn, the LORD will require the blood at his hand. Ezekiel is told he is such a watchman for Israel.

l: wicked man, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 33
s: The wicked who are not warned will die in their iniquity, with the watchman held accountable for their blood. The LORD takes no pleasure in their death and calls them to turn. A wicked person who turns, restores the pledge, returns robbed goods, and walks in the statutes of life will surely live, and his sins will not be remembered.

l: the righteous, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 33
s: The righteous are told their past righteousness will not deliver them on the day they sin. If one trusts in his righteousness and commits iniquity, none of his righteous deeds will be remembered and he will die in his iniquity. This shows that the righteous who turn from righteousness will die therein.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 33
s: In the twelfth year of the captivity, in the tenth month, on the fifth day, a man who had escaped out of Jerusalem comes to Ezekiel and reports that the city has been defeated.

l: land of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 33
s: The LORD vows to make the land a desolation and an astonishment, ending the pride of its power and leaving its mountains so desolate that no one passes through. This is because of the abominations of its people, and the people will then know that he is the LORD. Those in the waste places claim it as their inheritance, but the LORD questions whether they should possess it.

l: inhabitants of the waste places, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 33
s: Those living in the waste places of the land of Israel argue that since Abraham was one and inherited the land, they, being many, surely have it as their inheritance. The LORD answers that they eat with the blood, lift their eyes to idols, shed blood, stand on their sword, commit abominations and defile their neighbors' wives. He declares they will fall by the sword, be devoured by animals in the open field, or die of pestilence in strongholds and caves.

l: sword, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 33
s: The sword is the instrument of judgment the LORD brings on a land, which the watchman must warn of by blowing the trumpet. It is said to take away those who ignore the warning. The LORD also declares that those in the waste places will fall by the sword.

l: individual responsibility and repentance, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 33
s: The chapter teaches that each person is judged by his own ways: past righteousness does not save one who sins, and past wickedness does not condemn one who turns and does what is lawful and right. Those who hear a warning and ignore it bear their own blood, and a watchman who warns has delivered his soul. The LORD calls everyone to turn, turn from evil and live, and rejects the claim that his way is unfair.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 34
s: In Chapter 34 the LORD commands the prophet to speak against the shepherds of Israel, who feed themselves, eat the fat, and wear the wool while neglecting the sheep, ruling them with force so that they are scattered and become prey. The LORD declares that he is against these shepherds, will require his sheep from them, and will stop them from feeding on the flock. He promises to search for and gather his scattered sheep from the peoples and countries, bring them to their own land, and shepherd them with good pasture, healing the weak and destroying the fat and strong. He will judge between fat and lean sheep, rams and male goats, because the strong trample the pasture and push the diseased away. He will set up his servant David as one shepherd and prince, make a covenant of peace, bless the land, break the yoke of their enslavers, and affirm that they are his people and he is their God.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 34
s: The LORD pronounces woe on the shepherds of Israel, declares himself against them, and vows to require his sheep from their hand. He promises to search for, gather, feed, and shepherd his scattered flock himself, to judge between sheep and sheep, and to set up his servant David over them. He will make a covenant of peace, send showers of blessing, break the yoke of their oppressors, and be known as their God.

l: shepherds of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 34
s: The shepherds are condemned for feeding themselves, eating the fat and clothing themselves with wool, while failing to strengthen, heal, bind up, bring back, or seek the sheep, and instead ruling them with force and rigor. The LORD declares he is against them, will require his sheep from them, and will make them cease from feeding the sheep so that the flock is delivered from their mouth.

l: sheep (the LORD's flock, Israel), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 34
s: The sheep were scattered over the mountains and the whole earth for lack of a shepherd and became prey and food for the animals of the field. The LORD promises to rescue, gather, feed, and heal them, and to judge between fat and lean sheep, since the strong have trampled the pasture, fouled the water, and pushed the diseased away. They will dwell securely, no longer be prey, and know that the LORD is with them and they are his people, the sheep of his pasture.

l: Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 34
s: Israel is the land and people whose shepherds failed them, and whose scattered flock the LORD will bring back to their own land, to the mountains of Israel, to feed on good pasture. The house of Israel will come to know that the LORD their God is with them and that they are his people.

l: David, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 34
s: The LORD calls David his servant and promises to set him up as the one shepherd over the flock, who will feed them and be their shepherd. He is also named as prince among them, while the LORD himself is their God.

l: scattering and regathering of the flock, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 34
s: The flock was scattered through all the mountains, high hills, and the surface of the earth because there was no shepherd, and no one searched or sought for them. The LORD promises to deliver them from all places of the cloudy and dark day, bring them out from the peoples and countries into their own land, and feed them there in security.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 35
s: In Chapter 35 the LORD commands the prophet, addressed as 'Son of man', to set his face against Mount Seir and prophesy against it. The LORD declares that He is against Seir and will make it a perpetual desolation, laying its cities waste and filling its mountains, hills, and valleys with the slain. The reasons given are Seir's perpetual hostility, its handing the children of Israel over to the sword in their calamity, and its claim that the 'two nations and two countries' would be its own, although the LORD was there. The LORD also says He has heard Seir's insults and boasts against the mountains of Israel. Because Seir rejoiced over Israel's desolate inheritance, the LORD will make Seir and all Edom desolate, so that they will know He is the LORD.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 35
s: The LORD commands the prophet to prophesy against Mount Seir and declares that He is against it. He swears to make it desolate, repay its anger and envy, and make Himself known among them when He judges. He states that He heard all of Seir's insults and boasts, and that the outcome will lead them to know that He is the LORD.

l: Mount Seir, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 35
s: Mount Seir is the target of the LORD's prophecy, accused of perpetual hostility, handing Israel over to the sword, claiming the two nations and countries as its own, and insulting and boasting against the mountains of Israel. It is sentenced to become a perpetual desolation with uninhabited cities, its travelers cut off and its hills, valleys, and watercourses filled with the slain.

l: Edom, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 35
s: Edom is named in the final verse together with Mount Seir: 'You will be desolate, Mount Seir, and all Edom, even all of it.' It will share in the desolation, and they will know that the LORD is the LORD.

l: Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 35
s: Israel, called the children of Israel and the house of Israel, was handed over to the power of the sword in the time of its calamity and the iniquity of the end. Its mountains were mocked as desolate and 'given to devour', and its inheritance was rejoiced over. The LORD was there in its land and answers on its behalf.

l: perpetual hostility (Seir's hostility toward Israel), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 35
s: Seir's perpetual hostility is the first ground of the LORD's judgment, expressed in giving Israel over to the sword in its calamity. Because Seir did not hate blood, blood will pursue it, and the LORD will act according to its anger, envy, and hatred.

l: desolation (judgment on Seir), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 35
s: The LORD pledges to make Mount Seir a desolation and an astonishment, a perpetual desolation with cities uninhabited and its land full of the slain. It is measured against Seir's own rejoicing over Israel's desolation: 'as you rejoiced... so I will do to you.' It extends to all Edom and leads them to know that the LORD is the LORD.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 36
s: In Ezekiel 36 the Lord GOD commands the prophet to speak to the mountains of Israel, promising to punish Edom and the residue of the nations who mocked and seized the land. He promises that the mountains will bear fruit, be tilled, and be repopulated by the house of Israel, and will no longer devour or bereave their people. He explains that Israel defiled the land, was scattered among the nations, and profaned his holy name there. He declares he will act for the sake of his name, gathering them, cleansing them, giving them a new heart and his Spirit, and restoring the land to be like the garden of Eden so the nations will know he is the LORD.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 36
s: The Lord GOD speaks in jealousy and wrath against the nations and Edom, and swears that they will bear their shame. He declares he will act not for Israel's sake but for his holy name, gathering his people, cleansing them, giving them a new heart and his Spirit, and rebuilding the waste places so that the nations will know he is the LORD.

l: mountains of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 36
s: The mountains of Israel are addressed by the prophet and told to hear the LORD's word, having been mocked by the enemy and made a prey and derision. The Lord GOD promises they will shoot out branches and yield fruit, be tilled and sown, be inhabited by multiplied men and animals, and never again devour or bereave their nation or bear the shame of the nations.

l: house of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 36
s: The house of Israel defiled their land by their ways, deeds, bloodshed, and idols, and profaned God's holy name among the nations. God promises to gather them, cleanse them, give them a new heart and spirit, and make them his people again, after which they will remember their evil ways and loathe themselves. He also says he will be inquired of by them and will increase them like a flock.

l: land of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 36
s: The land of Israel was defiled by its inhabitants and made desolate, and the nations claimed it as a possession. God promises it will be tilled, free from famine, with cities inhabited and ruins rebuilt, so that it is said to have become like the garden of Eden.

l: residue of the nations, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 36
s: The residue of the nations, along with all Edom, took the land for themselves with joy and despite of soul, swallowed it up, and made it a prey and a derision. The Lord GOD speaks against them in the fire of his jealousy and swears they will bear their own shame. Those left around Israel will come to know that the LORD built the ruined places and planted what was desolate.

l: cleansing of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 36
s: God promises to sprinkle clean water on Israel and cleanse them from all their filthiness and idols. He will give them a new heart and new spirit, remove the stony heart, put his Spirit within them, and cause them to walk in his statutes. This is done for the sake of his holy name, and they will afterward remember their evil ways and loathe themselves.

l: scattering of Israel among the nations, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 36
s: God states that he poured out his wrath on Israel for their bloodshed and idols, scattering them among the nations and judging them according to their ways and deeds. Among the nations they profaned his holy name, since men said that they were the LORD's people who had left his land. This leads God to act out of respect for his name by gathering them from all the countries and bringing them back to their own land.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 37
s: In a vision, the LORD's Spirit sets the prophet, called son of man, in a valley full of very dry bones and tells him to prophesy over them. The bones assemble, gain sinews, flesh and skin, and then live and stand as a great army when breath comes at his prophesying to the wind. The LORD explains that the bones are the whole house of Israel, who say their hope is lost, and promises to open their graves, put his Spirit in them, and bring them into the land of Israel. He then has the prophet join two sticks, one for Judah and one for Joseph/Ephraim, as a sign that the divided nations will become one nation under one king. The LORD promises that David his servant will be their prince forever, that they will be cleansed from idols, and that he will make an everlasting covenant of peace and set his sanctuary among them.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 37
s: The LORD GOD brings the prophet by his Spirit to the valley, commands him to prophesy, and causes the bones to come together and live through breath. He promises to open Israel's graves, put his Spirit in his people, gather them from the nations into their land, unite them as one nation, cleanse them, and make an everlasting covenant of peace, setting his sanctuary among them so the nations will know he is the LORD who sanctifies Israel.

l: Ezekiel (son of man), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 37
s: Addressed as son of man, he is carried by the LORD's Spirit into the valley of bones, answers 'Lord GOD, you know' when asked if the bones can live, and prophesies to the bones and to the wind as commanded. He is then told to write on two sticks and join them into one in his hand, and to explain this to the people who ask what it means.

l: valley of bones, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 37
s: The valley is where the LORD sets the prophet down, and it is full of very many dry bones in the open. There the bones are reassembled and raised to life as an exceedingly great army.

l: dry bones, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 37
s: At the prophet's prophesying the dry bones come together bone to bone, gain sinews, flesh and skin, and then receive breath, live, and stand on their feet as an exceedingly great army. The LORD says they represent the whole house of Israel, who say their bones are dried up and their hope is lost.

l: house of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 37
s: The whole house of Israel is identified with the bones and is quoted as saying, 'Our bones are dried up, and our hope is lost. We are completely cut off.' The LORD promises to open their graves, put his Spirit in them, bring them into their own land, make them one nation under one king, cleanse them from idols, and dwell among them forever.

l: breath (wind), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 37
s: The bones have no breath in them after receiving sinews, flesh and skin, so the prophet is told to prophesy to the wind to come from the four winds and breathe on the slain. The breath enters them and they live and stand up.

l: land of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 37
s: The LORD promises to bring his people up from their graves into the land of Israel, to place them in their own land, and to gather them there from among the nations. He says they will be one nation on the mountains of Israel and will dwell in the land he gave to Jacob his servant forever, along with their children and their children's children.

l: Judah, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 37
s: Judah is named on the first stick the prophet writes: 'For Judah, and for the children of Israel his companions.' The LORD says he will put the stick of Joseph with the stick of Judah to make them one stick in his hand, signifying the end of the division between two nations.

l: Joseph, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 37
s: Joseph is named on the second stick, 'For Joseph, the stick of Ephraim, and for all the house of Israel his companions.' The LORD promises to take the stick of Joseph, in the hand of Ephraim, and join it with the stick of Judah so they become one in his hand.

l: sticks, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 37
s: The prophet writes on two sticks, one for Judah and one for Joseph/Ephraim, and joins them into one stick in his hand before the people's eyes. They are a sign that the LORD will make the divided Israel one nation, no longer two kingdoms.

l: David, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 37
s: The LORD calls David his servant and promises that he will be king over the united people and their one shepherd. He will also be their prince forever, as they dwell in the land and walk in the LORD's ordinances and statutes.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 38
s: In Ezekiel 38, the LORD tells Ezekiel (addressed as son of man) to prophesy against Gog, prince of Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal, of the land of Magog. The LORD says he will turn Gog around, bring him out with a vast army and allies including Persia, Cush, Put, Gomer, and Togarmah, and send him in the latter years against Israel, a land restored and dwelling securely in unwalled villages. Gog will devise an evil plan to seize plunder, while Sheba, Dedan, and the merchants of Tarshish question his motives. The LORD declares that he is bringing Gog against his land so the nations may know him when he is sanctified in Gog, and that his wrath will cause a great shaking, with swords turned against brothers, pestilence, blood, torrential rain, hailstones, fire, and sulfur. Through this judgment the LORD will magnify and sanctify himself and be known to many nations.

l: Gog, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 38
s: Gog, prince of Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal of the land of Magog, is declared an adversary of the LORD, who will turn him around, put hooks in his jaws, and bring him out. He will devise an evil plan to take plunder from Israel's unwalled villages, and the LORD says he is the one spoken of long ago by the prophets. He and his hordes will face judgment by sword, pestilence, blood, rain, hailstones, fire, and sulfur.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 38
s: The LORD commissions Ezekiel to prophesy against Gog and declares himself against him. He says he will bring Gog against his land in the latter days so that he may be sanctified in Gog before the nations' eyes. In jealousy and wrath he will shake the land, call for a sword against Gog, and judge him, making himself known as the LORD to many nations.

l: Ezekiel (son of man), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 38
s: Ezekiel, addressed as son of man, receives the LORD's word and is told to set his face toward Gog and prophesy against him. He is commanded to deliver the message twice, including telling Gog that the LORD will bring him against Israel.

l: Gog's army and allied peoples, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 38
s: Gog's force includes horses and horsemen in full armor, with bucklers, shields, and swords, along with Persia, Cush, Put, Gomer and all his hordes, and the house of Togarmah from the far north. They will come like a storm and a cloud covering the land, but they will be struck by the LORD's judgment, with every man's sword against his brother and torrential rain, hailstones, fire, and sulfur falling on them. Sheba, Dedan, and the merchants of Tarshish are separately shown questioning whether Gog has come for plunder.

l: Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 38
s: Israel is described as a land brought back from the sword and gathered out of many peoples onto its once continually wasted mountains. Its people dwell securely in unwalled villages without bars or gates, with livestock and goods, which draws Gog's plan to plunder them. The LORD calls them his people and his land.

l: Gog's invasion of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 38
s: The invasion is foretold for after many days, in the latter years, when Gog and many peoples ride from the far north like a storm and a cloud to cover the land. Gog's motive is to take plunder and prey from a secure, restored people. The LORD says he himself brings Gog against his land so the nations will know him.

l: God's judgment on Gog, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 38
s: When Gog comes against Israel, the LORD's wrath will rise, causing a great shaking in which creatures and men tremble, mountains are thrown down, and every wall falls. He will call a sword against Gog so that every man's sword is against his brother, and will judge him with pestilence, blood, torrential rains, great hailstones, fire, and sulfur. The result is that the LORD magnifies and sanctifies himself and is known to many nations.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 39
s: The Lord GOD commands the prophet to prophesy against Gog, prince of Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal, announcing that he will draw Gog from the far north onto the mountains of Israel, disarm him, and cause him and his hordes to fall and be devoured by birds and animals. Israel will burn the enemy weapons for seven years and bury Gog's multitude in the valley of Hamon Gog for seven months to cleanse the land, with continual searchers marking any remaining bones. The birds and animals are summoned to a great sacrifice on the mountains of Israel, where they will eat the flesh and drink the blood of mighty men, princes, horses, and charioteers. The Lord GOD declares that the nations will see his glory and judgment and will understand that Israel went into captivity for its iniquity. He promises to reverse the captivity of Jacob, show mercy to the whole house of Israel, gather them to their land, and pour out his Spirit on them, never hiding his face from them again.

l: Gog, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 39
s: Gog, prince of Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal, is declared an enemy of the Lord GOD, who will turn him around and bring him from the uttermost parts of the north onto the mountains of Israel. His bow and arrows are struck from his hands, and he and all his hordes and allied peoples fall in the open field. He is given a burial place in Israel, the valley of Hamon Gog, where he and his multitude are buried.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 39
s: The Lord GOD declares himself against Gog, strikes down him and his hordes, sends fire on Magog and the island dwellers, and summons the birds and animals to his sacrificial feast. He vows to make his holy name known and no longer profaned, to set his glory among the nations, and to reverse Israel's captivity. He explains that he hid his face from Israel for its iniquity, but promises not to hide it again since he has poured out his Spirit on them.

l: Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 39
s: Israel will burn the weapons of the fallen army as fuel for seven years, plunder those who plundered them, and bury Gog's multitude for seven months to cleanse the land. They will come to know the Lord as their God from that day forward. Their captivity will be reversed, they will receive mercy, forget their shame, dwell securely, and receive the Lord's Spirit.

l: mountains of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 39
s: The mountains of Israel are the place where the Lord GOD brings Gog and where Gog and his hordes fall. They are also the site of the great sacrifice to which the birds and animals are invited to eat flesh and drink blood.

l: valley of Hamon Gog, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 39
s: The valley of Hamon Gog is the burial place the Lord GOD gives to Gog in Israel, located in the valley of those who pass through on the east of the sea, where it will stop travelers. Gog and all his multitude are buried there, and it receives its name from this. Bones found by searchers are marked and buried there, and a city will be called Hamonah.

l: nations, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 39
s: The nations will know that the Lord is the LORD, the Holy One in Israel, and will see his judgment and the hand he has laid on them. They will also learn that Israel went into captivity for its iniquity and trespass, not because of any weakness of God. The Lord will be shown holy among Israel in the sight of many nations.

l: birds and animals (of Gog's slaughter), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 39
s: Birds of every sort and animals of the field are given Gog and his hordes to be devoured. They are summoned to assemble from every side and eat meat and drink blood until full and drunk at the Lord's table.

l: great sacrifice (the feast on the mountains of Israel), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 39
s: The Lord GOD calls the great sacrifice he prepares on the mountains of Israel, where birds and animals will eat the flesh of the mighty and drink the blood of the princes of the earth. The feast includes rams, lambs, goats, bulls, fatlings of Bashan, and horses, charioteers, mighty men, and men of war.

l: burial of Gog's army (cleansing the land), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 39
s: The house of Israel and all the people of the land will bury Gog's multitude for seven months to cleanse the land, and this will make them famous in the day the Lord is glorified. Men of continual employment will then pass through the land to search for remaining bones, setting up a sign by each until the undertakers bury it in the valley of Hamon Gog.

l: Israel's captivity, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 39
s: The Lord explains that the house of Israel went into captivity for their iniquity and trespass, as he hid his face and gave them into the hand of their adversaries, and they fell by the sword. He promises to reverse the captivity of Jacob, gather them from the peoples and enemy lands, and leave none of them captive any more.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 40
s: Chapter 40 opens in the twenty-fifth year of the captivity, when the LORD's hand brings the speaker, addressed as son of man, in visions of God to a very high mountain in the land of Israel, where there is something like the frame of a city. A man with the appearance of bronze, holding a line of flax and a measuring reed, charges him to see, hear, and set his heart on all he is shown and to declare it to the house of Israel. The man measures the wall, the east gate with its lodges, porch, posts, windows, and palm trees, then the outer court with its pavement and thirty rooms, and the north and south gates of the outer court, each fifty cubits long and twenty-five wide with seven steps. He then measures the matching gates of the inner court, each reached by eight steps, along with the rooms where burnt offerings were washed, the eight tables for killing sacrifices, and the four cut stone tables. Finally he describes the rooms for singers and for priests, identifying the sons of Zadok as those who minister to the LORD, and measures the square inner court, the altar before the house, and the porch of the house.

l: Ezekiel (son of man), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 40
s: In the twenty-fifth year of the captivity, the LORD's hand brings him in visions of God to a very high mountain in the land of Israel. He is told to see with his eyes, hear with his ears, and set his heart on all that is shown, and to declare it all to the house of Israel.

l: the man with the measuring reed (guide), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 40
s: He appears with the look of bronze, holding a line of flax and a measuring reed, and stands in the gate. He guides the speaker through the outer and inner courts, measures every gate, court, and porch, and explains that the south-facing room is for the priests who perform the duty of the house and the north-facing room for those who perform the duty of the altar.

l: the temple, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 40
s: Its porch is measured last: twenty cubits long and eleven wide, with steps leading up to it and pillars by the posts on each side. Each post of the porch is five cubits on either side, and the gate's width is three cubits on each side. The altar stands before the house.

l: east gate, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 40
s: It is the first gate measured. The man goes up its steps and measures its thresholds, lodges, porch, posts, and opening. It has three side rooms on each side of one measure, closed windows, and palm trees on each post, and is fifty cubits long and twenty-five wide in the surrounding measurements.

l: north gate of outer court, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 40
s: Its lodges (three on each side), posts, arches, windows, and palm trees match the measure of the east gate, and it is fifty cubits long and twenty-five wide. It is reached by seven steps, with its arches before them. A gate to the inner court faces it, one hundred cubits away.

l: south gate of outer court, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 40
s: The man leads the speaker south and measures its posts and arches by the same measurements, with windows all around, a length of fifty cubits and a width of twenty-five. It has seven steps up to it, arches before them, and palm trees on its posts. One hundred cubits separate it from the south gate of the inner court.

l: outer court, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 40
s: The man brings the speaker into it and shows rooms and a pavement all around, with thirty rooms on the pavement. The pavement lies beside the gates, matching their length, and is called the lower pavement. The width from the lower gate to the inner court's forefront is one hundred cubits on the east and north.

l: inner court, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 40
s: It is entered by gates on the south, east, and north, each measured by the same standard as the others. It is a square one hundred cubits long and one hundred wide. The altar stands before the house in it, and rooms for singers and priests lie within it.

l: inner gates, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 40
s: The south, east, and north gates of the inner court are each measured by the same measurements, with lodges, posts, arches, and windows all around, fifty cubits long and twenty-five wide. Their arches face the outer court, palm trees stand on their posts, and each is reached by eight steps.

l: sacrificial tables, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 40
s: Two tables stand on each side in the gate porch, with more outside the north entry, making four on each side and eight in all for killing the burnt, sin, and trespass offerings. Four cut stone tables, a cubit and a half square and one cubit high, hold the instruments of slaughter. Hooks a hand width long are fastened within, and the meat of the offering lies on the tables.

l: measurements of the temple, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 40
s: The man measures with a reed of six cubits, each cubit a cubit and a hand width. The wall is one reed thick and one reed high. Gate thresholds and lodges are one reed, and the gates are fifty cubits by twenty-five, with courts and gate-to-gate distances of one hundred cubits.

l: vision of the new temple, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 40
s: The vision is given in the twenty-fifth year of the captivity, fourteen years after the city was struck, and shows a structure like a city frame on a very high mountain. This chapter covers the gates, courts, offering tables, priests' rooms, and the house's porch. The speaker is commanded to declare all of it to the house of Israel.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 41
s: Chapter 41 describes a guide measuring the parts of the temple for the narrator, beginning with the nave, its posts, and its entrance, and then the inner room he calls the most holy place. It details the wall of the house and the three-story side rooms built into it, along with the raised base, open area, and the separate place and building at the west. The guide gives overall dimensions of one hundred cubits for the temple, the separate place with its building, and the east face. The walls and doors are decorated with cherubim and palm trees, each cherub having a man's face and a young lion's face. The chapter ends with the wooden altar, called the table before the LORD, and the two-leaved doors of the temple and sanctuary.

l: the temple, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 41
s: The temple is measured as one hundred cubits long, and its east face is one hundred cubits wide together with the separate place. Its walls are decorated throughout with cherubim and palm trees from the ground to above the door. It and the sanctuary have two doors, each with two turning leaves.

l: nave, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 41
s: The guide measures the nave's posts at six cubits on each side, and its entrance at ten cubits wide, with a length of forty cubits and a width of twenty cubits. Its door posts are squared, and its face looks like that of the temple. Its doors carry cherubim and palm trees like those on the walls, with a wooden threshold on the porch's face outside.

l: most holy place, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 41
s: After going inward, the guide measures the entrance posts and entrance of the inner room. He gives its length and width as twenty cubits each, before the nave, and tells the narrator, "This is the most holy place."

l: side rooms (of the house), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 41
s: The side rooms are four cubits wide all around the house, in three stories with thirty in each story, set into the house wall so as not to penetrate it. They grow wider on higher levels as the walls narrow, and one climbs through the middle level to the highest. Their doors open toward an open area five cubits wide, one door to the north and one to the south.

l: separate place (behind the temple), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 41
s: The building before the separate place on the west side is seventy cubits wide with walls five cubits thick, and ninety cubits long. The separate place and the building with its walls together measure one hundred cubits long. The separate place's east face is counted as one hundred cubits wide with the temple.

l: cherubim, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 41
s: Cherubim alternate with palm trees on the walls throughout the house, from the ground to above the door. Each cherub has two faces: a man's face toward the palm tree on one side and a young lion's face toward the palm tree on the other. They are also made on the nave's doors.

l: altar, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 41
s: The altar is made of wood, three cubits high and two cubits long, with corners, base, and walls of wood. The guide tells the narrator, "This is the table that is before the LORD."

l: the man with the measuring reed (guide), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 41
s: The guide brings the narrator to the nave and measures the posts, entrances, walls, side rooms, and the building behind. He goes inward to measure the inner room and tells the narrator it is the most holy place. He also identifies the wooden altar as the table before the LORD.

l: measurements of the temple, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 41
s: The measurements include a nave twenty cubits wide and forty long, an inner room of twenty by twenty cubits, a house wall of six cubits, and side rooms of four cubits. The raised base is a full reed of six great cubits, and the open area is five cubits. The temple and the separate place with its building each measure one hundred cubits in length, and the east face measures one hundred cubits.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 42
s: In Ezekiel 42 the speaker is led by a guide into the outer court toward the north, where he sees a building of rooms arranged in three stories of galleries, with the upper rooms set back and shorter than the lower ones. The north building is one hundred cubits long and fifty wide, with an entry on the east side, and matching rooms lie to the south and east. The guide explains that these are holy rooms where priests who are near the LORD eat and lay the most holy things: the meal offering, sin offering, and trespass offering. Priests must leave their ministering garments in these rooms and put on other garments before approaching the people. After finishing the inner house, the guide measures the whole surrounding area through the east gate, finding five hundred reeds on each of the four sides, and notes a wall five hundred cubits by five hundred cubits that separates the holy from the common.

l: the man with the measuring reed (guide), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 42
s: He brings the speaker out into the outer court toward the north and into the rooms opposite the separate place. He explains that the north and south rooms are holy and states the priests' rules. After finishing the inner house, he leads the speaker out by the east gate and measures all four sides of the surrounding area with the measuring reed.

l: Ezekiel (son of man), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 42
s: He is brought by the guide into the outer court and the north rooms, where he observes the galleries, doors, and dimensions. He is told by the guide what the rooms are for and what the priests must do there. He then accompanies the guide as the whole area is measured.

l: sons of Zadok, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 42
s: Priests who are near to the LORD eat the most holy things in the holy rooms. When they enter, they may not go out of the holy place into the outer court until they lay down the garments in which they minister, because those garments are holy. They then put on other garments before approaching what is for the people.

l: outer court, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 42
s: The guide brings the speaker out into the outer court toward the north. The rooms there are fifty cubits long, and the entry to the rooms on the east side is reached from the outer court. Priests must not go out into it from the holy place until they have changed their garments.

l: holy rooms (north and south rooms), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 42
s: The north building is one hundred cubits long and fifty wide, with a north door, three stories of galleries, and upper rooms shorter than the lower and middle ones because the galleries take space from them. Rooms on the south and east have a similar arrangement of doors and dimensions. The guide declares the north and south rooms holy, as places where priests eat and lay the most holy things.

l: most holy things (offerings), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 42
s: The most holy things, including the meal offering, the sin offering, and the trespass offering, are eaten by the priests and laid in the holy rooms. The place is called holy for this reason.

l: walls and enclosure (500-cubit wall), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 42
s: A wall surrounds the measured area, five hundred cubits long and five hundred cubits wide. A wall in the thickness of the court toward the east also has rooms, and a wall outside the rooms toward the outer court is fifty cubits long.

l: measurement of the surrounding area, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 42
s: After finishing the inner house, the guide leads the speaker out by the east gate and measures all around with the measuring reed. The east, north, south, and west sides each measure five hundred reeds, so the area is measured on all four sides.

l: separation between holy and common, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 42
s: The wall around the five-hundred-cubit square exists to make a separation between that which is holy and that which is common. The priests' changing of garments before approaching the people reflects the same distinction.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 43
s: In Chapter 43 the narrator is brought to the east gate, where the glory of the God of Israel returns from the east, enters the house by that gate, and fills the house after the Spirit lifts him into the inner court. A voice from the house declares it the place of God's throne where he will dwell forever among the children of Israel, provided they stop defiling his name with prostitution and the dead bodies of their kings. The narrator is told to show the house's form and laws to the house of Israel so they may be ashamed and keep its ordinances. The altar's measurements are given, including its base, ledges, four horns, twelve-cubit hearth, and east-facing steps. Finally, God sets out a seven-day rite of sin offerings, a young bull, and a ram, with blood and salt, for the Levitical priests of Zadok's offspring to cleanse and consecrate the altar, after which God will accept the people's offerings on the eighth day.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 43
s: The God of Israel declares the house to be the place of his throne and the soles of his feet, where he will dwell among the children of Israel forever. He states that he consumed them in anger for their abominations, and he promises to dwell among them if they put away their prostitution and the kings' dead bodies. He gives the altar's ordinances and promises to accept the people once the consecration is completed.

l: the glory of the God of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 43
s: The glory of the God of Israel comes from the east with a voice like many waters, and the earth is illuminated by it. It enters the house by the east-facing gate and fills the house. Its appearance matches the earlier visions, including the one by the river Chebar.

l: Ezekiel (son of man), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 43
s: The narrator is brought to the east gate, sees the glory approach, and falls on his face. The Spirit lifts him into the inner court, where he hears a voice from the house while a man stands beside him. He is commanded to show the house to Israel, make known its form and laws, and write them in the people's sight.

l: house of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 43
s: The house of Israel is told it will no more defile God's holy name, neither the people nor their kings, through prostitution and the kings' dead bodies. They are to put these away and be shown the house so they may be ashamed of their iniquities and measure the pattern. They are to keep and do its ordinances, and they will be accepted when their offerings are made on the altar.

l: the temple, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 43
s: The house is filled with the LORD's glory after the glory enters by the east gate. It is called the place of God's throne, and its whole limit on the mountain top is declared most holy. Its form, exits, entrances, structure, ordinances, and laws are to be shown and written down for Israel.

l: east gate, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 43
s: The east gate is where the narrator is brought and where the glory of the God of Israel arrives from the east. The LORD's glory enters the house by way of this gate, which faces east.

l: the altar, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 43
s: The altar is given detailed measurements: a base, a lower ledge, a greater ledge, an upper altar of four cubits, four horns, a twelve-by-twelve cubit hearth, and a fourteen-by-fourteen ledge, with its steps facing east. Its ordinances cover offering burnt offerings and sprinkling blood on it. It is to be cleansed and made atonement for over seven days, after which it is consecrated.

l: sons of Zadok, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 43
s: The Levitical priests of the offspring of Zadok are described as those near to God who minister to him. They receive a young bull for a sin offering, and they cast salt on the offerings. On the eighth day and onward, they are to make the people's burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar.

l: altar consecration offerings, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 43
s: The consecration begins with a young bull as a sin offering, with its blood put on the four horns, the four corners of the ledge, and the border, and the bull burned outside the sanctuary. On the second day a male goat without defect is offered, and then a young bull and a ram without defect are offered as burnt offerings with salt. For seven days a goat, a young bull, and a ram are prepared each day, and on the eighth day the regular burnt and peace offerings begin.

l: abominations and defilement of the sanctuary, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 43
s: Prostitution and the dead bodies of kings in their high places are named as the defilement of God's holy name, along with setting their threshold and door post beside his. God says this left a wall between him and the people, and that he consumed them in anger for these abominations. Israel is told to put them away far from him so that he may dwell among them forever.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 44
s: In Chapter 44, the speaker is brought back to the outer east gate of the sanctuary, which the LORD declares must stay shut because the LORD, the God of Israel, entered by it; only the prince may sit in its porch to eat bread before the LORD. At the north gate the speaker sees the LORD's glory fill the house and falls on his face, then is told to mark carefully all the house's ordinances. The LORD rebukes the house of Israel for bringing uncircumcised foreigners into the sanctuary and bars them from entering. The Levites who went astray after idols will bear their iniquity and be limited to guarding the gates and serving the people, while the Levitical priests, the sons of Zadok, who kept the sanctuary's duty, may approach the LORD to offer fat and blood. The chapter ends with rules for those priests' clothing, hair, wine, marriage, teaching, judging, contact with the dead, inheritance, portions of offerings, and forbidden food.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 44
s: The LORD declares the east gate must remain shut because he entered by it, and his glory fills his house. He rebukes Israel for admitting foreigners into his sanctuary, lifts his hand against the idolatrous Levites, and appoints the sons of Zadok to approach him. He sets rules for priests and says he himself is their inheritance and possession.

l: Ezekiel (son of man), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 44
s: The speaker is brought by the east gate and then the north gate, where he sees the LORD's glory fill the house and falls on his face. He is addressed as 'Son of man' and told to mark well, see, and hear all the ordinances and laws, and to tell the rebellious house of Israel the LORD's words.

l: Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 44
s: The house of Israel is called rebellious and rebuked to stop its abominations, including bringing uncircumcised foreigners into the sanctuary and setting others to perform the duty of the holy things. Its people are to be taught the difference between holy and common and clean and unclean. They are to give the priests offerings, first fruits, and the first of their dough.

l: Levites, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 44
s: The Levites who went far from the LORD after idols, and ministered to the people before idols, will bear their iniquity and shame. They may not act as priests or come near the holy and most holy things. They are made ministers with oversight at the gates, who kill the burnt offering and sacrifice for the people and perform the house's service.

l: sons of Zadok, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 44
s: The Levitical priests, the sons of Zadok, are commended for performing the duty of the sanctuary when Israel went astray. They alone may come near to minister to the LORD, offer the fat and blood, enter the sanctuary, and approach his table. They are bound by the regulations on dress, hair, wine, marriage, teaching, judging, and the dead, and receive offerings as their portion.

l: foreigners (uncircumcised in heart and flesh), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 44
s: Foreigners uncircumcised in heart and flesh were brought by Israel into the sanctuary when the bread, fat, and blood were offered, profaning the house and breaking the covenant. The LORD decrees that no such foreigner among the children of Israel shall enter his sanctuary.

l: east gate of the sanctuary, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 44
s: The outer east gate of the sanctuary is shown shut. The LORD says it must stay shut and unopened, with no man entering by it, because the LORD, the God of Israel, has entered by it. Only the prince may sit in it to eat bread before the LORD, entering and leaving by the porch of the gate.

l: sanctuary (the LORD's house), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 44
s: The LORD's house is filled with the LORD's glory, seen from the north gate. Its ordinances, laws, entrances, and exits are to be carefully marked. It has been profaned by foreigners and is now to be served only by the appointed Levites at its gates and the sons of Zadok within, with inner and outer courts and holy rooms.

l: priestly garments and grooming regulations, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 44
s: Priests entering the inner court gates must wear linen garments, linen turbans, and linen trousers, with no wool and nothing that causes sweat. They must change into other clothes and leave their ministering garments in the holy rooms before going to the outer court, so they do not sanctify the people. They may not shave their heads or let their locks grow long, may not drink wine entering the inner court, and may marry only virgins of Israel or a priest's widow.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 45
s: Chapter 45 gives instructions for dividing the land by lot, with a holy portion of 25,000 by 10,000 reeds set aside as an offering to the LORD. Within it lie the sanctuary and its pasture lands, a section for the priests, and a section for the Levites, alongside a city possession for the whole house of Israel and land on either side for the prince. The LORD rebukes the princes of Israel for violence, plunder, and dispossessing his people, and commands just balances and consistent measures for the ephah, bath, homer, shekel, and mina. The people are to give a set offering of wheat, barley, oil, and lambs, and the prince is made responsible for providing the burnt, meal, drink, sin, and peace offerings at feasts, new moons, and Sabbaths. The chapter ends with the cleansing of the sanctuary on the first day of the first month, the Passover on the fourteenth day with seven days of unleavened bread and daily offerings, and a matching seven-day feast in the seventh month.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 45
s: The LORD commands that a holy portion of the land be offered to him when the land is divided by lot. He rebukes the princes of Israel for oppression, demands justice and just measures, and prescribes offerings and feasts to make atonement for the house of Israel.

l: land of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 45
s: It is set apart as an offering to the LORD, 25,000 reeds long and 10,000 wide, holy in all its border. It contains the sanctuary, the priests' portion, and the Levites' portion, and lies beside the city possession.

l: sanctuary (in the holy portion), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 45
s: The sanctuary is most holy and sits within the holy portion, on a 500 by 500 square with fifty cubits of pasture lands all around. The priests' portion serves as a place for their houses and a holy place for it.

l: sons of Zadok, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 45
s: The priests, who come near to minister to the LORD, receive a holy portion of the land as a place for their houses and for the sanctuary. A priest also puts the blood of the sin offering on the house's door posts, the corners of the altar ledge, and the gate posts of the inner court.

l: Levites, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 45
s: The Levites, ministers of the house, are given a portion 25,000 cubits long and 10,000 wide as their possession, for twenty rooms.

l: house of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 45
s: The whole house of Israel receives the city possession, 5,000 wide and 25,000 long, next to the holy portion. The princes are to give the land to the house according to tribes, and the prince's offerings make atonement for it.

l: prince, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 45
s: The prince receives land on both sides of the holy allotment and city possession, from the west border to the east border. He must no longer oppress the people, and he is responsible for providing the offerings at feasts, new moons, and Sabbaths. At Passover he prepares a bull for sin offering for himself and the people and supplies the daily offerings.

l: just weights and measures, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 45
s: The LORD requires just balances, a just ephah, and a just bath. The ephah and bath are to be of one measure, each a tenth of a homer, the shekel is twenty gerahs, and the mina is twenty plus twenty-five plus fifteen shekels.

l: offering of grain, oil and lamb, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 45
s: The people of the land are to give a sixth of an ephah from a homer of wheat and of barley, a tenth of a bath of oil from the cor, and one lamb from every two hundred of the flock. These serve for meal, burnt, and peace offerings to make atonement, and are given for the prince.

l: sacrifices (burnt, meal, sin, peace, drink offerings), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 45
s: The prince is to provide these offerings at feasts, new moons, Sabbaths, and appointed feasts to make atonement for the house of Israel. During the seven days of Passover, daily offerings are seven bulls, seven rams, and a male goat for a sin offering, with a meal offering of an ephah per bull and ram and a hin of oil per ephah.

l: cleansing of the sanctuary (first month), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 45
s: On the first day of the first month a young bull without defect is taken to cleanse the sanctuary. The priest puts its blood on the house's door posts, the altar ledge's four corners, and the inner court gate posts, and the rite is repeated on the seventh day for those who err or are simple, to make atonement for the house.

l: Passover, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 45
s: It is held on the fourteenth day of the first month as a seven-day feast with unleavened bread. The prince prepares a sin offering bull on the first day and daily burnt and sin offerings through the seven days. A similar seven-day feast is held from the fifteenth day of the seventh month with the same provisions.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 46
s: Chapter 46 gives the Lord GOD's regulations for worship and land in the restored temple. The east gate of the inner court is shut on the six working days but opened on the Sabbath and the new moon, when the prince worships at its threshold while the priests prepare his offerings and the people of the land worship at its door. Specified burnt offerings and meal offerings are set for the Sabbath, the new moon, and the feasts, along with a daily morning lamb as a continual burnt offering. The prince may give gifts from his own inheritance to his sons permanently, to servants only until the year of liberty, and must never take the people's inheritance.
