A guide then shows the narrator the holy rooms for the priests, where sin and trespass offerings and meal offerings are cooked, and the corner courts with boiling houses where the ministers boil the people's sacrifices.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 46
s: The Lord GOD speaks the regulations on the gate, the prince's offerings, the daily offering, and the prince's inheritance. He requires offerings without defect and ordains the daily offering as a perpetual ordinance, and he wants his people not to be scattered from their possessions.

l: prince, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 46
s: The prince enters by the porch of the east gate on the Sabbath and new moon, stands by the post, and worships at the threshold, going out the same way. He provides the prescribed offerings, may offer free will offerings through the opened east gate, goes in and out with the people at feasts, and is bound by laws forbidding him to seize the people's inheritance.

l: priests (of the temple), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 46
s: The priests prepare the prince's burnt offering and peace offerings. They use the holy rooms on the north side to boil the trespass and sin offerings and bake the meal offering so these are not carried into the outer court to sanctify the people.

l: people of the land, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 46
s: The people of the land worship at the door of the east gate before the LORD on Sabbaths and new moons. At appointed feasts they enter by the north or south gate and must leave by the opposite gate, going straight ahead, with the prince going in and out among them.

l: east gate, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 46
s: The gate is shut on the six working days and opened on the Sabbath and the new moon. It is also opened for the prince's free will offerings, and it is not shut until evening, or after he has gone out.

l: outer court, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 46
s: The guide brings the narrator out into the outer court and leads him past its four corners. The priests are to keep the sacrificial portions from being carried out into it, so that the people are not sanctified by them.

l: corner courts, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 46
s: Each of the four corners of the outer court contains an enclosed court forty cubits long and thirty wide, all the same size. A wall surrounds them, and boiling places are built under the walls all around.

l: boiling houses, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 46
s: The guide identifies the boiling places in the corner courts as boiling houses. There the ministers of the house boil the sacrifices of the people.

l: holy rooms (north and south rooms), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 46
s: The guide brings the narrator through the entry at the side of the gate to these rooms, which face north and have a place at the back toward the west. There the priests boil the trespass and sin offerings and bake the meal offering.

l: Sabbath, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 46
s: On the Sabbath the east gate of the inner court is opened. The prince's burnt offering that day is six lambs and a ram without defect, with a meal offering of an ephah for the ram, as much as he can give for the lambs, and a hin of oil to an ephah.

l: new moon, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 46
s: The east gate is opened on the day of the new moon, and the people worship at its door. The prince's offering is a young bull, six lambs, and a ram, all without defect, with an ephah of meal for the bull and for the ram and a hin of oil to an ephah.

l: burnt offering, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 46
s: Burnt offerings are prescribed for the Sabbath, the new moon, and the prince's free will offerings, always of animals without defect. The priests prepare them for the prince, and a lamb a year old is offered daily.

l: meal offering, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 46
s: Meal offerings accompany the animal offerings: an ephah for the bull or ram, as much as the prince is able for the lambs, and a hin of oil to an ephah. The priests bake the meal offering in the holy rooms to keep it from the outer court.

l: daily continual burnt offering, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 46
s: A lamb a year old without defect is prepared every morning as a burnt offering to the LORD. With it go a meal offering of a sixth of an ephah and a third of a hin of oil to moisten the fine flour, as a perpetual ordinance.

l: prince's inheritance laws, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 46
s: A gift from the prince's inheritance to his sons stays theirs as a possession. A gift to a servant returns to the prince at the year of liberty, and the prince may not take the people's inheritance to drive them out, but must give his sons inheritance from his own possession.

l: man (guide), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 46
s: The guide, who speaks to the narrator, brings him through the entry to the holy rooms for the priests and explains their use. He then leads him through the outer court past its four corners and explains that the corner structures are boiling houses.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 47
s: In Ezekiel's vision, a man with a measuring line leads him back to the temple door, where water flows out from beneath the threshold eastward, south of the altar. The man measures off four stretches of one thousand cubits, and the water deepens from ankle-deep to knee-deep to waist-deep to a river too deep to cross. Along its banks grow very many trees, and the man explains that the waters will flow into the Arabah and the sea, healing it so that every living creature and a great multitude of fish live, though the swamps and marshes will be given up to salt. The Lord GOD then sets out the borders of the land (north, east, south, and west) to be divided by lot among the twelve tribes, with Joseph having two portions. The aliens living among Israel and fathering children there are to be treated as native-born and receive an inheritance in whatever tribe they live.

l: the temple, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 47
s: Waters flow out from under the threshold of the temple eastward, since its front faces east, coming down on the south side of the altar. The temple is the source of the river, and the trees' fruit and leaves are said to flourish because the waters issue out of the sanctuary.

l: river (flowing from the temple), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 47
s: The river flows eastward from the temple and deepens over each thousand cubits measured, from ankle-deep to knee-deep to waist-deep, until it is too deep to walk through. It will go down into the Arabah and into the sea, healing the waters and bringing life to every creature wherever it comes, though its swamps and marshes will remain salt.

l: the man with the measuring reed (guide), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 47
s: The man leads Ezekiel out by the northern gate and around to the outer east gate, then measures one thousand cubits at a time with the line in his hand. He has Ezekiel pass through the waters at each depth, asks whether he has seen this, and explains where the waters go and what they will do.

l: Ezekiel (son of man), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 47
s: Addressed as "Son of man," Ezekiel is brought back to the temple door and led through the waters at ankle, knee, and waist depth until the river is too deep to cross. He is then returned to the bank, where he sees the many trees, and hears the man explain the river's healing effect.

l: trees (along the river), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 47
s: Very many trees stand on both banks of the river. Every tree for food will grow there, with leaves that do not wither and fruit that does not fail, producing new fruit every month because the waters come from the sanctuary; the fruit is for food and the leaf for healing.

l: the sea (Dead Sea), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 47
s: The river's waters flow into the sea, which will be made to flow out, and its waters will be healed. Fish will multiply in great numbers there, with fishermen spreading nets from En Gedi to En Eglaim, though its swamps and marshes will not be healed but given up to salt.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 47
s: The Lord GOD declares the border by which the land is to be divided for inheritance among the twelve tribes, with Joseph receiving two portions. He states that he swore to give the land to the fathers of Israel, and that the aliens are to receive inheritance among the tribes.

l: Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 47
s: The twelve tribes of Israel are told to divide the land for inheritance by lot, each receiving a portion, with Joseph having two. They are to treat the aliens who live among them and father children there as native-born, giving them an inheritance among the tribes.

l: land of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 47
s: The land is to fall to Israel as an inheritance, as the Lord GOD swore to give it to their fathers. It is to be divided by lot among the tribes, and also to the aliens who live among them.

l: aliens (strangers among Israel), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 47
s: The aliens who live among Israel and father children among them are to be regarded as native-born among the children of Israel. They are to share in the inheritance, receiving their portion in whatever tribe they live.

l: borders of the land, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 47
s: The north border runs from the great sea by way of Hethlon to the entrance of Zedad, and on to Hamath, Berothah, Sibraim, Hazer Hatticon, and Hazar Enon at the border of Damascus. The east side is the Jordan, between Hauran, Damascus, Gilead, and the land of Israel, to the east sea; the south runs from Tamar to the waters of Meriboth Kadesh, to the brook, to the great sea; and the west side is the great sea.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 48
s: Chapter 48 describes how the land is divided among the tribes of Israel by lot, with seven tribal portions from Dan to Judah in the north, and five more from Benjamin to Gad in the south. Between Judah and Benjamin lies a central square offering of twenty-five thousand by twenty-five thousand reeds, containing the holy offering for the priests of the sons of Zadok with the sanctuary in its middle, an adjoining portion for the Levites, and the city with its farmland. The prince receives the remaining land on either side of the offering and the city. The chapter also lists the city's measurements and its twelve gates named after the tribes, and closes by giving the city the name 'The LORD is there.'

l: Dan, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 48
s: Dan is the first tribe named, receiving one portion at the far north end beside the way of Hethlon, the entrance of Hamath, and Hazar Enan at the border of Damascus. Dan also gives its name to one of the three east gates of the city.

l: tribes of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 48
s: The tribes each receive one portion running east to west, and those who labor in the city out of all the tribes cultivate the city's land. The twelve city gates are named after the tribes, with Joseph, Levi and Benjamin among them.

l: priests, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 48
s: The priests, described as sanctified sons of Zadok who kept the LORD's instruction and did not go astray when Israel and the Levites did, receive the holy offering of twenty-five thousand by ten thousand with the sanctuary in its middle. It is a most holy thing, bordering the Levites' portion.

l: Levites, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 48
s: The Levites receive a portion alongside the priests' border, twenty-five thousand in length and ten thousand in width. They may not sell or exchange any of it, nor alienate the first fruits of the land, because it is holy to the LORD. They are said to have gone astray when Israel went astray.

l: prince, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 48
s: The prince receives the remainder of the land on both sides of the holy offering and the city's possession, eastward and westward to the borders. His land also lies between the border of Judah and the border of Benjamin, around the Levites' and the city's possessions.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 48
s: The LORD is the one to whom the offering is made and to whom the Levites' land is holy. The land is declared to be divided by lot according to the word of the Lord GOD. The city is finally named 'The LORD is there.'

l: holy offering, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 48
s: The holy offering measures twenty-five thousand reeds by ten thousand and is set apart for the priests, with the sanctuary in its middle. Together with the Levites' portion and the city's possession it forms a square of twenty-five thousand by twenty-five thousand.

l: sanctuary (in the holy portion), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 48
s: The sanctuary of the LORD is placed in the middle of the offering that lies in the portion beside Judah's border. It is also in the middle of the land belonging to the prince.

l: city, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 48
s: The city lies in the middle of the five-thousand-cubit strip left over, for common use, dwelling and pasture. It measures four thousand five hundred on each side, has two hundred fifty of pasture lands around it, and eighteen thousand in circumference. It has three gates on each side named after the tribes, and from that day its name is 'The LORD is there.'

l: land of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 48
s: The land is to be divided by lot among the tribes of Israel for inheritance. Its southern border runs from Tamar to the waters of Meribath Kadesh, to the brook, and to the great sea.

l: tribal portions, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 48
s: Twelve tribal portions are laid out as east-west strips, seven from Dan to Judah in the north and five from Benjamin to Gad in the south. Each tribe has one portion, and Gad's border forms the southern boundary of the land.

l: The Book of Obadiah, The Book of Obadiah, The Book of Obadiah / Chapter 1
s: Obadiah's vision records the LORD's judgment against Edom, also called Esau, whose pride in its high rocky dwelling leads it to think no one can bring it down. The LORD says he will make Edom small, bring it down from its heights, and destroy its wise men and mighty men, including those of Teman. Edom is condemned for violence against its brother Jacob: it stood aside while strangers plundered Jerusalem, and it rejoiced, seized wealth, and cut off escapees. The day of the LORD is near for all the nations, and what they have done will return on their own heads. Mount Zion will have those who escape, the house of Jacob will be a fire consuming the house of Esau, and the possessions of Esau and other lands will be taken, ending with the kingdom belonging to the LORD.

l: Edom, The Book of Obadiah, The Book of Obadiah / Chapter 1
s: Edom, also called Esau, is told it has been made small and despised, and that pride in its high rocky dwelling has deceived it. Its allies and friends betray it, its wise and mighty men are destroyed, and it is cut off forever for violence against Jacob and for standing aside, rejoicing, and plundering when Jerusalem fell. The house of Esau becomes stubble burned by Jacob, with none remaining, and its mountain is possessed by those of the South and judged by saviors from Mount Zion.

l: LORD, The Book of Obadiah, The Book of Obadiah / Chapter 1
s: The LORD speaks against Edom, saying he will bring it down even from among the stars and destroy its wise men and understanding. He declares that the day of the LORD is near for all the nations and that deeds will be repaid. He has spoken that none will remain of the house of Esau, and the kingdom will be his.

l: Jacob, The Book of Obadiah, The Book of Obadiah / Chapter 1
s: Jacob is Edom's brother, against whom Edom committed violence, and whose Jerusalem and children of Judah suffered disaster and plunder. In the end the house of Jacob will possess its possessions and be a fire, with the house of Joseph a flame, that devours the house of Esau.

l: Mount Zion, The Book of Obadiah, The Book of Obadiah / Chapter 1
s: Mount Zion is where there will be those who escape, and it will be holy. Saviors will go up on Mount Zion to judge the mountains of Esau.

l: day of the LORD, The Book of Obadiah, The Book of Obadiah / Chapter 1
s: The day of the LORD is said to be near for all the nations. On it, as they have done will be done to them, and their deeds will return on their own heads.

l: nations, The Book of Obadiah, The Book of Obadiah / Chapter 1
s: The nations are told that an ambassador has been sent among them to rise up against Edom in battle, and Edom is made small among them. The day of the LORD is near for all the nations, who as they drank on God's holy mountain will drink continually, swallow down, and be as though they had not been.

l: The Book of Joshua
s: The Book of Joshua, in 24 chapters, follows Israel's entry into, conquest of, and settlement in the promised land under Joshua, son of Nun, who succeeds Moses. The LORD, Joshua, Rahab, Achan, Caleb, Eleazar the priest, and the tribes matter most. Chapters 1-5 cover the preparation and crossing. The LORD commands Joshua to be strong and keep the law, and the eastern tribes pledge to obey him. Two spies are sheltered in Jericho by Rahab, who is promised protection for her household. The priests carry the ark into the Jordan, the waters stop, and Israel crosses on dry ground. Twelve stones are set up as a memorial. At Gilgal the people are circumcised and keep Passover, the manna ceases, and Joshua meets the commander of the LORD's army. Chapters 6-12 recount the conquest. Jericho's wall falls after a seven-day march, and Rahab's household is spared. Achan takes devoted things, Israel is defeated at Ai, and Achan is stoned. Ai is then taken by ambush, and Joshua reads the law at Ebal and Gerizim. The Gibeonites trick Joshua into a covenant and become servants. A southern coalition is routed, with hailstones and the sun standing still, and a northern coalition under Jabin of Hazor is also defeated. Chapter 12 lists thirty-one defeated kings west of the Jordan alongside Sihon and Og in the east. Chapters 13-21 describe the division of the land. Joshua is old, and much land remains. The eastern tribes already hold their inheritance, and Levi receives cities rather than territory. Caleb, aged eighty-five, receives Hebron, and Othniel wins Debir and Achsah. Lots are cast for Judah, Ephraim, Manasseh, Benjamin, and the remaining tribes, mostly at Shiloh. Zelophehad's daughters receive an inheritance. Some Canaanites are not driven out. Six cities of refuge are set apart, and forty-eight Levite cities are assigned. The text declares that none of the LORD's promises failed. Chapters 22-24 conclude the book. The eastern tribes return home and build an altar by the Jordan. War is averted when Phinehas and the princes accept it as a witness. Joshua gives a farewell charge warning against intermarriage and foreign gods. At Shechem he recounts Israel's history, the people pledge to serve the LORD, and he makes a covenant and sets up a stone. Joshua and Eleazar die and are buried, and Joseph's bones are buried at Shechem.

l: Joshua, The Book of Joshua
s: Joshua, son of Nun, is the servant of Moses and later servant of the LORD, who succeeds Moses as leader of Israel. Commissioned by the LORD in the opening chapter to lead the people across the Jordan, he is told to be strong, courageous and faithful to the law, and the eastern tribes pledge to obey him as they did Moses. The LORD magnifies him in the sight of all Israel so that they fear him all his days as they feared Moses, and his fame spreads through the land because the LORD is with him. His story unfolds in three phases. First, conquest: he sends spies to Jericho, moves the people to the Jordan, sets up twelve memorial stones, circumcises Israel, and meets the armed man near Jericho whom he worships and obeys. He carries out the LORD's plan against Jericho, saves Rahab's household, and curses anyone who rebuilds the city. After the defeat at Ai he laments, sanctifies the people, and Israel executes judgment on Achan. He then takes Ai by ambush, builds an altar on Mount Ebal, and reads the law to the assembly. He makes a covenant with the deceiving Gibeonites, then makes them wood cutters and water drawers. He defeats the five kings, as the sun and moon stand still, destroys the southern cities, and takes Hazor and the northern land, leaving nothing undone of what the LORD commanded Moses. He camps at Gilgal. Second, division of the land: old and advanced in years, he is commanded to divide the remaining land among the nine tribes and half-tribe of Manasseh. With Eleazar and the tribal heads he distributes inheritances by lot, giving Hebron to Caleb, addressing the children of Joseph, sending surveyors, casting lots at Shiloh, and relaying the command about cities of refuge. He himself receives Timnathserah, which he builds and lives in. He blesses and sends home the eastern tribes. Third, farewell: he gathers Israel's leaders, urges courage, faithfulness and love for the LORD, and says he is going the way of all the earth. At Shechem he recounts the LORD's acts, declares that he and his house will serve the LORD, makes a covenant, writes the words in the book of the law, and sets up a witness stone. He dies at 110 and is buried in Timnathserah in Ephraim's hill country.

l: LORD, The Book of Joshua
s: The LORD is the God of Israel, presented throughout the Book of Joshua as a living, holy, jealous God and Lord of all the earth, whose mighty hand fulfills oaths sworn to Israel's fathers. At the start he speaks to Joshua after Moses' death, commanding him to cross the Jordan and be strong, promising his presence as with Moses, and pledging never to fail or forsake him. Rahab recalls that he dried up the Red Sea and gave Israel the land. He then magnifies Joshua by cutting off the Jordan's waters for the crossing, a sign that the living God is among Israel and a testimony that his hand is mighty and to be feared. He commands the renewed circumcision, rolls away the reproach of Egypt, and recalls swearing that the disobedient exodus generation would not see the land. In conquest he delivers Jericho, Ai and the southern and northern enemies into Israel's hand, giving battle instructions, throwing great stones from the sky, hardening the peoples' hearts, and fighting for Israel. Jericho's silver, gold, bronze and iron are holy to him and belong in his treasury. His anger burns when Achan's trespass in the devoted things brings defeat, and it turns away after judgment. Israel's failure to ask his counsel binds it to the Gibeonite oath sworn in his name. He directs the division of land by lot, remains the inheritance of Levi in place of land, spares and honors Caleb who wholly followed him, and commands cities of refuge. He gives Israel rest on all sides and fulfills every good thing he promised, and he pledges to drive out the remaining nations. Joshua's farewells warn that disobeying the covenant will kindle his anger and bring evil until Israel is destroyed from the land. Joshua recounts his history from Abraham through the exodus and conquest, calling him holy and jealous, who will not forgive those who forsake him. Israel serves him throughout the days of Joshua and the elders who outlived him.

l: Moses, The Book of Joshua
s: Moses is presented in the Book of Joshua as the deceased servant of the LORD and man of God, whose authority and commands continue to shape Israel's conquest and land division. Chapter 1 opens with his death: the LORD promises to be with Joshua as with Moses, his law and command about land beyond the Jordan are invoked, and the eastern tribes pledge to heed Joshua as they heeded Moses. Chapter 11 shows Joshua carrying out Moses' commands, which Moses received from the LORD, in destroying the cities and inhabitants. Chapter 12 recalls Moses striking Sihon and Og with the Israelites and giving their east-of-Jordan land to Reuben, Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh. Chapter 13 adds that he gave these Transjordan inheritances in the plains of Moab, drove out Og's remnant of the Rephaim, struck Sihon with the chiefs of Midian, and gave Levi no inheritance. Chapter 14 credits him as the channel for the lot-based division, recalls the eastern inheritances, and notes he sent Caleb to spy out the land and swore the land Caleb walked would be his and his children's forever.

l: Jordan, The Book of Joshua
s: The Jordan is a river that overflows all its banks at harvest time and serves as a boundary between the eastern tribes (Reuben, Gad, half of Manasseh) and the rest of Israel. In Joshua 1, Joshua and the people are told to cross it within three days. In chapter 3, as the priests' feet touch its edge, its waters stand in a heap far upstream at Adam, leaving dry ground. In chapter 4, the people cross, twelve stones are taken from and set in its midst, and the waters return over its banks. In chapter 22, it remains the dividing line, and the eastern tribes fear it will be said the river leaves them no portion in the LORD.

l: promised land (land given to Israel), The Book of Joshua
s: The promised land is territory the LORD swears to give the children of Israel, as pledged to their fathers. Bounded by the wilderness and Lebanon north-south, the Euphrates east, and the great sea west, it includes the Hittites' land; Joshua receives every place his foot treads.

l: children of Israel, The Book of Joshua
s: The children of Israel are the people to whom the LORD gives the land of Canaan, led by Joshua and commanded to fear and worship the LORD forever. The records trace their move from promise to settlement. Told to prepare food, they sanctify themselves, follow the ark, and cross the Jordan on dry ground near Jericho while the priests stand in the river. Forty thousand armed men from Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh cross before the LORD. They encamp at Gilgal on the tenth day of the first month, fearing Joshua as they had feared Moses. There they are circumcised at the LORD's command, keep the Passover, and eat the land's produce as the manna ceases. Jericho is shut up because of them; they are warned against taking devoted things, and Rahab and her family are brought out and live among Israel. They are then recorded as having struck the kings east of the Jordan with Moses, possessing the land from the valley of the Arnon to Mount Hermon, and the thirty-one kings west of the Jordan with Joshua. The land is divided by lot among nine and a half tribes as the LORD commanded Moses, and the Levites receive only cities with pasture lands, after which the land rests from war. The whole congregation assembles at Shiloh and sets up the Tent of Meeting. Three men per tribe survey the land, and the division is finished by borders and lot before the LORD. They give Joshua Timnathserah, which he asked for. They assign cities of refuge for themselves and the alien among them. Finally, hearing of an altar, they gather at Shiloh for war against the eastern tribes, but first send Phinehas and ten princes. Satisfied by the explanation, they bless God and abandon the war.

l: Reubenites, The Book of Joshua
s: The Reubenites are a tribe of Israel who received their inheritance east of the Jordan from Moses, sharing the region with Gad and half of Manasseh. Their land, bordered by the Jordan's bank, ran from Aroer by the Arnon valley and included Heshbon, Dibon, Jahaz, Beth Peor, the plain cities and Sihon's kingdom. In Joshua 1 they are reminded to leave families and livestock behind while their fighting men cross ahead of their brothers, and they pledge obedience to Joshua as to Moses. In chapter 22 Joshua releases them to Gilead, where they build an altar by the Jordan, defending it as a witness that the LORD is God.

l: Gadites, The Book of Joshua
s: The Gadites are a tribe who received their inheritance east of the Jordan from Moses, shared in Gilead with Reuben and the half-tribe of Manasseh. Their territory included Jazer, the cities of Gilead, half the Ammonite land, Mahanaim, Succoth and other places, reaching to the sea of Chinnereth. In Joshua 1 they pledge to obey Joshua and send armed men across to help their brothers. In chapter 13 their land is described. In chapter 22 Joshua sends them home, and they build a witness altar by the Jordan, defended and vindicated by Phinehas.

l: half-tribe of Manasseh, The Book of Joshua
s: The half-tribe of Manasseh is one portion of Manasseh that Moses settled east of the Jordan, in Bashan, Og's former kingdom, including Jair's sixty villages and part of Gilead shared with Reuben and Gad. Joshua addresses it with Reuben and Gad, and its fighting men pledge obedience and agree to cross the Jordan armed to help their brothers. The other half receives land west of the river. Afterward Joshua dismisses it with a blessing; it returns east, helps build the great altar, and is cleared of trespass after explaining the altar's purpose.

l: book of the law of Moses, The Book of Joshua
s: The book of the law of Moses is a written law authored by Moses, containing blessing and curse. Moses commanded it to Joshua, who is told it must not leave his mouth, to meditate on it day and night, and to follow it without turning right or left, in order to prosper. Joshua later writes a copy on stones, builds an altar accordingly, and reads all its words to the assembly. Finally he urges Israel to keep it courageously.

l: crossing of the Jordan, The Book of Joshua
s: scheduled_within three days [people to cross to possess the land] The LORD commands Joshua to arise and cross the Jordan with all the people into the land. Joshua has the officers tell the people to prepare food because they will cross within three days. The armed men of the eastern tribes are to cross ahead of their brothers.

l: Rahab, The Book of Joshua
s: Rahab is a prostitute living in a house on Jericho's wall who believes the LORD is God in heaven and on earth. She hides two spies under flax on her roof, misleads the king's messengers, and asks the spies to swear to spare her family. She lowers them by a cord and ties a scarlet line in her window. When Jericho is destroyed, she and her father's household are brought out alive and saved, and she lives in the middle of Israel to this day.

l: two spies (sent by Joshua), The Book of Joshua
s: Two spies, sent by Joshua for the children of Israel, scout Jericho, are sheltered and hidden by Rahab, swear kindness with scarlet-thread conditions, hide three days in the mountain, then report the inhabitants' fear.

l: king of Jericho, The Book of Joshua
s: rules Jericho The king of Jericho is told that Israelite men have come to spy out the land and sends to Rahab demanding that she bring them out. He is deceived by her, and his pursuers chase the spies toward the fords of the Jordan without finding them.

l: Jericho, The Book of Joshua
s: Jericho is a walled city with a king and inhabitants, first viewed by spies sent to it, whose gate is shut at dark. Rahab reports its people's hearts have melted in fear of Israel. The Israelites keep Passover in its plains, and Joshua meets a man with a drawn sword nearby. The city is tightly shut up, the LORD gives it to Joshua, its wall falls flat after the shout, and it is devoted to destruction, burned. Joshua curses anyone who rebuilds it with the loss of firstborn and youngest sons.

l: Sihon, The Book of Joshua
s: Sihon was an Amorite king beyond the Jordan who lived in Heshbon and ruled from Aroer at the Arnon valley's edge, over half of Gilead to the Jabbok and the eastern Arabah. His territory bordered Og's. Moses and the Israelites struck him, utterly destroying him.

l: Og, The Book of Joshua
s: Og was an Amorite king of Bashan, a remnant of the Rephaim, living at Ashtaroth and Edrei. He ruled Mount Hermon, Salecah, all Bashan, and half of Gilead bordering Sihon. Moses and the Israelites struck and utterly destroyed him.

l: Rahab's family (Rahab's father's house), The Book of Joshua
s: Rahab asks that her father, mother, brothers, sisters, and all they have be saved alive from death. The spies agree to protect those who are with her in the house, and instruct her to gather her father, mother, brothers, and all her father's household inside; whoever goes out into the street will bear their own blood.

l: scarlet thread (Rahab's window sign), The Book of Joshua
s: is_located_in Rahab's window [sign marking the house to be spared] The spies tell Rahab to tie a line of scarlet thread in the window she used to let them down, as the sign for when they come into the land. She ties the scarlet line in the window after sending them away.

l: oath (Rahab and the spies' oath), The Book of Joshua
s: binds two spies (sent by Joshua) [guiltless if Rahab talks or family leaves the house] Rahab asks the spies to swear by the LORD to deal kindly with her father's house, and they agree, pledging their lives for hers if she does not talk about their business. They declare themselves guiltless of the oath if she speaks of it, or if anyone leaves her house, and she accepts the terms.
